items.question: Direction: why product engineering (guide profile)
items.answer:
Neerav moved from research into product engineering to put his research skills to work where they change outcomes: building rigorous systems with innovative interaction design and real evaluation layers, aimed at education, healthcare, and workflow automation. His research years taught him to define a measurable question, control the conditions, and keep the evidence inspectable, first in the peer-reviewed OpenCV atrophy method and then in the four-class MRI ensemble experiment. Product engineering lets him apply that discipline to systems people use every day, where the interaction itself decides whether the rigor reaches the user.

Each product carries that direction into a specific domain:

- Education and research: Refract turns findings from learning science and research methods into product mechanics. Answer-before-reveal recall, confidence captured before feedback, versioned grading, FSRS scheduling, and review-gated statistics let the product record whether learning and analysis actually improved.
- Healthcare: Homeward brings the care of the imaging research into a patient workflow. Every recovery task is bound to its exact source, uncertainty stays explicit as durable state, and deterministic services keep authority over clinical wording, dates, and approvals.
- Workflow automation: Relay and the Deep Strat LLM workflow turn ambiguous service requests into structured, confirmed, verified outcomes, with versioned evaluation that converts each failure into an engineering fix.

Interaction design is part of that rigor. Relay's voice guide moves the page to the evidence it used, Refract makes recall visible before the answer appears, Homeward shows the source behind every step, and Birb Hangout builds consent and co-presence into its social interactions. The thread across his work is consistent: a research question about what helps people, an interaction that makes the answer natural to use, and an evaluation layer that shows whether it worked.

items.question: Homeward: lessons and next version (guide project record)
items.answer:
Three lessons from building Homeward carry directly into its next version.

Contract-first design is what made the safety model testable. Defining discharge review, next-step selection, source trust, role capabilities, approval, and failure behavior as explicit contracts, and sharing scenario functions between the domain tests and the evaluation runner, meant every guardrail case exercised the real product path. The next version starts from those contracts and the scenario matrix before any new interface work.

The deterministic paths are the foundation of the product. Provider rejection showed that plan navigation, lexical source search, saved-record summaries, citations, and care-team coordination keep a patient moving without any model, and the specialists add value on top of that baseline. Each new agent capability follows the same pattern: the model selects, and the application decides.

Uncertainty belongs in the data model. Missing dates, conflicting uploads, unreviewed imports, and open help requests became durable state with their own transitions, which is what let the product stay honest under pressure. Keeping that modeling discipline as the product grows is the core of its quality.

The path to launch changes the environment around the product: authenticated patients and care teams in place of a local care-team operator, real discharge records in place of fictional material and synthetic Synthea history, and clinical validation with care partners.

items.question: How does Relay stop the model from taking unsafe actions?
items.answer: Relay keeps authority out of the model. The model can only prepare a typed proposal, and the server issues a confirmation token bound to the resolved employee, the action, its arguments, and the record revision. Each write is idempotent, logged in audit history, and checked against the resulting state. In 21 recorded safety runs, there were zero unsafe state changes.

items.question: Walk me through how a Relay request goes from voice to a confirmed action.
items.answer: Relay's voice guide turns a spoken need into a typed proposal, and the employee's explicit confirmation is what triggers the write. Speech is recognized by Deepgram and reasoned over by GPT-4.1, and the guide resolves the request against the signed-in employee's records. For a consequential request, the server prepares the action and the employee sees exactly what will happen. The confirmation token is bound to that employee, the action, its arguments, and the record revision. The write is idempotent, it leaves an audit event, and the app checks the visible result before reporting success.
